_what_this_is: The entry gate, answered BEFORE drafting. The threshold question is whether a well-informed non-expert would confidently believe something the primary sources do not support.

belief._note: What the reader already believes, stated as they would state it. If you cannot write this sentence, there is nothing to correct and no subject -- which is how the tobacco-analogy candidate died.
belief.statement: Programmes to include disabled children in school in poorer countries generally help. Inclusive education, where disabled children learn in mainstream classrooms with trained teachers, works better than separate special schools. Cheap fixes like glasses, hearing aids or ramps make a big difference. But most children with disabilities in these countries are still out of school or learning very little.
belief.how_we_know_they_believe_it: The coverage that settled it. Named outlets, quoted headlines. Not 'it is widely assumed'.

carried_by.by: a model's reading (claude-sonnet-4-6, web search), verified by code: the page was fetched with the honest client and contains the belief's key words

what_the_sources_show.statement: The review held finds that a range of individual-level interventions work to improve educational outcomes for people with disabilities in LMICs, but that there is little research on systemic or school-level change.
what_the_sources_show.by: a model's reading (claude-opus-5-5, from held sources), the quotation verified verbatim by code

direction._note: CORRECTS, CONFIRMS or NARROWS. This field exists so the contrarianism guard can count. A publication whose answer is always CORRECTS is performing scepticism rather than assessing evidence, and is not to be trusted.
direction.by: a model's reading (claude-opus-5-5, from held sources), the quotation verified verbatim by code
direction.why: The sources support the idea that interventions generally help, mainly individual-level ones, but they do not show inclusive settings working better than specialist ones, and they note that some impairments, such as deafness, may benefit from separate instruction.

reader_with_a_decision: A programme officer at a donor, NGO or education ministry in a low- or middle-income country deciding which disability-education interventions to fund or scale (for example teacher training for inclusion, assistive devices, community-based rehabilitation, cash transfers, or special or resource units), and whether the evidence is strong enough to commit to one approach over another.

public_record_check._note: NOT 'has anybody published this'. On any contested question, somebody has. The question is whether it has been carried WHERE THIS READER WOULD FIND IT. Run the counterexample hunter on the belief statement, not on the finding.
public_record_check.carried_in_general_coverage: Yes: Their World (https://key.theirworld.org/resources/inclusion-and-disability), fetched 2026-11-25, sha256 8e8ae8f32468e25d; the page contains 23 of the belief's 34 key words. A model's reading (web search), checked by code.
public_record_check.our_contribution: translation, extension, or correction of the prior art -- say which

kill_condition: Rigorous primary evaluations (randomised or well-controlled studies measuring enrolment, attendance or learning for disabled children in LMICs) are numerous and broadly consistent. They show clear positive effects, and they rank intervention types the way the common belief does, so careful reading adds nothing beyond 'yes, and inclusive approaches work best'. Equally, there would be no story if there are almost no such evaluations, so the honest answer is simply 'unknown' with nothing further to report.

kill_condition_tested.by: a model's reading (claude-opus-5-5, from held sources), the quotation verified verbatim by code
kill_condition_tested.note: Evaluations exist and are mostly positive, but they are thin on enrolment and systemic approaches and do not rank inclusive above specialist settings, so neither the 'yes, inclusive works best' outcome nor the 'no evidence at all' outcome holds.

scope._note: What the answer will and will not cover, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened, so scope cannot be fitted to the findings afterwards. An omission ruled OUT_OF_SCOPE, and a headline conclusion declared out of scope, must name the question's words or one of these entries (fix 2, docs/whu-fix2-omission-rulings-design.md section 2.4).
scope.covers: Interventions delivered in low- and middle-income countries that aim to improve educational outcomes for children and young people with disabilities. Outcomes include enrolment, attendance, retention, progression, learning or achievement, and participation in school. Intervention types include school-level, teacher-level, child-level (including assistive technology and health interventions), family or community-level, and policy or financing approaches. The question also asks which types show larger or more reliable effects.

out.what: How many children with disabilities in LMICs are out of school, and how large the education gap is
out.why: That is a prevalence and descriptive question. This page is about whether interventions change outcomes.

out.what: Effectiveness of disability-education programmes in high-income countries
out.why: School systems, resources and service availability differ too much to pool or transfer the findings directly.

out.what: Whether inclusive education is a human right or required by the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities
out.why: That is a normative and legal question, not an empirical question about effectiveness.

out.what: Health or functional outcomes of rehabilitation and assistive devices where no education outcome is measured
out.why: The question concerns education. Purely clinical effects are a separate evidence base.
These need cost data that effectiveness evaluations rarely report. They would be a separate analysis.

out.what: Education programmes for all children that do not report results separately for children with disabilities
out.why: Without disaggregated results, effects on disabled children cannot be identified.

evidence_standard._note: What kinds of evidence the answer will weigh, written at step 1 BEFORE any source is opened (post-study fix 3, docs/whu-fix3-evidence-standard.md). 'measured': outcomes measured in trials, cohorts, evaluations. 'assessed': expert assessments -- systematic-review conclusions, IPCC confidence-rated statements, guideline recommendations. When they differ, the page states both and drops neither.
evidence_standard.measured: Effect estimates from primary studies, ideally randomised or quasi-experimental with a comparison group, on education outcomes for children and young people with disabilities in LMICs. Examples are changes in enrolment or attendance rates, test scores or learning gains, and dropout or progression. These come with sample sizes, effect sizes and confidence intervals, broken down by intervention type, impairment type, country and age.
evidence_standard.assessed: Certainty ratings and synthesis judgements from systematic reviews or evidence panels, such as GRADE certainty of evidence (high, moderate, low, very low) per intervention-outcome pair, risk-of-bias assessments, and a review's overall conclusion about whether an intervention type 'probably improves', 'may improve' or has 'uncertain' effects. These also include stated evidence gaps, as in an evidence gap map.
